In interpreting “the divine ones” as “sages and philosophers,” we rely on the Brethren of Purity themselves. For example, in Rasāʾil, vol. 4, pp. 301–302, they speak of “divine philosophical worship.” In their view, true “divinity” means philosophical wisdom, and the true “divine person” is the philosophical sage.↩︎

We have already explained the historical meaning of the word ṣanāʾiʿ on p. 288, footnote 53. We can add that in the terminology of the Brethren of Purity, people of the ṣanāʾiʿ are workers who produce socially useful goods. The phrase does not mean owners of the means of production, such as land, workshops, and other productive tools.↩︎

Malakiyya here comes from malāʾika, “angels.” The Brethren of Purity believed that the rank of angels is the highest level that righteous human souls can reach. Since they saw it as an “evolutionary” development of righteous human beings, it corresponds to the highest stage in their ascending “development” of living beings: from the vegetative faculty, to the rational faculty, and then to the angelic. See Rasāʾil, vol. 2, p. 172. They also connect nature with the angels. In their thought, angels are in fact an expression of the nature present in the Universal Soul. See Rasāʾil, vol. 2, pp. 55, 108–109.↩︎

In the Brethren’s treatise on “Definitions and Descriptions,” they define active nature as “a power of the Universal Celestial Soul flowing through the elements.” In their terminology, the “elements” are the primary elements of matter. See Rasāʾil, vol. 3, p. 363, section on psychology and intellect. Nature here is being defined as an abstract category.↩︎

Rasāʾil, vol. 4, p. 184. When the Brethren assign certain beliefs to the founder of the religious law and derive those beliefs from their own philosophical principles, this strongly suggests that the lawgiver they have in mind is not the Islamic Prophet, and that the “law” is not Islamic law. Rather, they seem to be trying to formulate a law of their own for the “State of the People of Good,” the state whose plan they outline in their encyclopedic Rasāʾil. We draw attention to this because it opens up several lines of inquiry. Our observation is strengthened by the fact that they also list twelve qualities that, in their view, the “founder of the law” must possess. All twelve are physical, moral, or intellectual qualities that could exist in any human being given healthy conditions of life. See Rasāʾil, vol. 4, pp. 172–173.↩︎

The wording speaks of “each existent thing,” which makes it seem as though the statement is not specifically about human beings. But the rest of the passage makes clear that it means an “existent” that acts consciously, voluntarily, and according to judgment. This applies only to the human being.↩︎
